draft.title: Conflicts after the Cold War
card: After the Cold War, several wars broke out inside states, not between them. The UN and major powers had to decide whether to step in.

Yugoslavia broke apart from 1991, and war followed in Croatia and Bosnia. UN peacekeepers were sent, but their mandate was limited and they could not stop attacks on civilians. In July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces killed over 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica, a town the UN had declared a safe area.

In 1994, Hutu extremists in Rwanda carried out a genocide in about 100 days, killing around 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi. A small UN force was already there, but it was not given the troops or the orders to stop the killing, and it was reduced in size as the violence grew. Major powers chose not to send large forces.
In both cases, the UN could act only as far as its member states were willing to give troops, money and a strong mandate. The UN's limits came from the will of states, not just from the UN itself.
draft.remember: In the 1990s the UN could only do what its member states were willing to back with troops and a firm mandate.

a.q: Which statement best explains why the UN failed to stop the genocide in Rwanda in 1994?
opts: Major powers were unwilling to send a strong force
The UN had no peacekeepers anywhere in Rwanda
The UN sent a large force, but it lost the fighting
Rwanda's government banned all foreign involvement
a.why: The UN force in Rwanda was small and was not given the troops or orders it needed, because major powers chose not to commit. The claim that no peacekeepers were present is wrong: a small UN force was already in the country.
a.clue: Think about who decides how many troops the UN gets.

b.q: A student argues that the UN's failures in Bosnia and Rwanda show a shared problem. Which statement best supports this argument?
opts: Member states gave the UN limited forces and mandates
Both conflicts were wars between two separate states
The UN had no role in either conflict at any stage
Both conflicts ended quickly once the UN arrived
b.why: In both Bosnia and Rwanda, UN forces were present but were limited by what states would provide and authorise. The UN did have a role in both, so saying it had none is wrong. Both conflicts were also fought inside states, not between them.
b.clue: Look for what both cases share: a UN presence that was held back.

a.best: Major powers were unwilling to send a strong force

b.best: Member states gave the UN limited forces and mandates

problems.detail: The clue 'a UN presence that was held back' all but names the correct option. Only one option describes the UN being held back, so the clue gives the answer away instead of prompting thinking.
